item.title: Escaping the "Gu" Education: A Survival Guide for Ordinary Families
item.description: In the current environment, education seems to have become a massive "jar" (or "vessel"), where children fight and engage in hyper-competition (or "involution") for limited resources. As parents, we feel heartbroken watching the light in our children's eyes slowly dim, yet we are compelled to fuel this process out of fear of being left behind.
item.content:encoded:
I. Seeing the Truth: The Fundamental Collapse of Educational Logic

  1. From “Changing the World” to “Securing the Rice Bowl”: The previous educational goal was to cultivate entrepreneurs and leaders, but the current social mindset has shifted toward seeking “stability” and the “iron rice bowl.” This signifies that the market pie has stopped growing.
  2. Degree Devaluation and Asset Shrinkage: The phenomenon of university graduates being unemployed or forced into manual labor is frequent (e.g., 1/4 of delivery riders hold a university degree). From an economic perspective, the return on investment for cultivating an ordinary white-collar worker for millions is now “catastrophic.”
  3. The Dimensional Strike of the AI Era: Chinese education excels at cultivating “perfect problem-solving machines,” but this skill—high execution ability coupled with low tolerance for error—is precisely what AI is most easily replacing.
  4. The Complete Collapse of Mental Health: Involution (excessive competition) has led to soaring rates of depression and suicide among youth year after year. Many children, despite gaining admission to prestigious schools, suffer from “hollow heart syndrome,” feeling that life lacks meaning.

II. Core Strategy: Installing a “Dual Operating System” for Children

If you cannot immediately emigrate or change your environment, do not choose a suicidal head-on confrontation. Instead, learn the Agent Mindset:

1. External System: Survival System (Efficient Compliance)

  • Role-Playing Mindset: Tell your child that school is a massive “scripted role-playing game” (Juběn Shā); the teachers are NPCs, and grades are in-game currency. The child is playing the role of a “good student,” but that doesn’t mean they are that student.
  • The Essence of Homework is “Stress Training”: Treat tedious, repetitive homework as a “willpower dumbbell.” It trains the ability to complete tasks even when you dislike them, rather than focusing solely on the knowledge itself.
  • Emotional Resilience and Task Separation: View a teacher’s criticism as a projection of their personal emotions, not a definition of the child’s personality; view a ranking as a data metric on a “cognitive health checkup,” not a personal evaluation.

2. Internal System: Life System (Independent Thinking)

  • Establish a Cognitive Isolation Zone: Textbook viewpoints are merely “passcodes prepared for scoring.” Encourage the child to question, to seek out the other side of the world through the internet and books.
  • Return to the Commoner’s Historical View: Avoid grand narratives. Take your child to understand the true history of your family, realizing that individual joys and sorrows are more real than cold, hard dates. This strengthens immunity against extreme ideologies.

III. The “Noah’s Ark” for the Future: True Skill Configuration

  1. English is “Information Sovereignty”: Learning English is no longer just about passing exams; it is about directly reading primary sources (such as YouTube science explainers or Google Scholar papers) to gain an advantage in the information gap.
  2. Mastering a “Hard Skill”: The ability to interact with the physical world (such as car repair, first aid, complex cooking, or electrical work) is the hardest thing for AI to replace. This is not just about a job; it is about anti-fragility in times of upheaval.
  3. Financial Acumen and Cycle Thinking: Instill the concept of a balance sheet from a young age, letting the child understand that money is “ice that melts.” Teach them to identify economic cycles and understand risk-taking rather than relying solely on labor for wealth.

IV. The Ultimate Responsibility of Parents: Becoming the “Artificial Kidney”

The home should be a safe harbor, not a second examination hall.

  • Filtering Toxins: Parents must swallow the anxieties of society and metabolize the shame and ranking pressure that school places on their children.
  • Building a Diversified Evaluation System: At home, heavily reward the ability to solve real-world problems (such as fixing the router or cooking independently). This ensures the child’s self-esteem is supported by multiple pillars; even if the pillar of grades falls, the person will not collapse.

💡 Supplement: Extended Methods

The following methods can more specifically help children build this resilience:

  1. “Dinner Table Debate”: Every week, choose a news topic and require your child to argue from the opposing side. This effectively counters the “standard answer” training of school and cultivates critical thinking.
  2. Low-Cost Trial-and-Error Experiments: Give your child a small sum of money (like New Year’s money) and let them decide to purchase a certain “asset” (such as a company’s stock or learning a new skill). If they lose money, don’t scold them; instead, review the “cycle” and the “choice,” making financial education practical.
  3. “Purpose-Free” Exploration Time: Mandatorily reserve 30–60 minutes daily for “white space time.” No problem-solving allowed; only activities the child is genuinely interested in and that have no immediate utility (even if it’s taking apart an old alarm clock). This is key to repairing “hollow heart syndrome.”
  4. Building a “Failure Archive”: Share your own professional failures with your child. Let them see that even when things fail, the sky doesn’t fall, and life continues. This builds a genuine sense of security better than any motivational story.

item.title: Children aren't meant to be tools for competition; they are simply the family's mirror.
item.description: An in-depth analysis of the family and social factors behind children's phone addiction and declining grades, calling for parents to self-reflect and grow, rather than merely "chicken-raising" (over-parenting/forcing them to excel).
item.content:encoded:
Children are not meant to be in the rat race; they are merely mirrors of the family

🪞【I】Is it because children have poor grades due to playing on their phones?

Whenever a child’s grades slip, the first reaction of parents is often: “Did they secretly play on their phone again?”

The phone seems to have become the culprit that ruins children. But have we ever considered that the logic of this problem might be completely reversed:

Children don’t have poor grades because they play on their phones; rather, they play on their phones because they have poor grades, lack choices, and lack companionship.

The phone is never the root cause of the problem; it is merely a manifestation of a lack of family resources. It is cheap, convenient, and easily addictive—it is the “only entertainment” many families can afford.

💡【II】The phone of the poor child vs. the equestrian hobby of the rich child

Imagine that every child has 6 hours of free time each day. Children from wealthy families might attend equestrian classes, swimming, piano lessons, play with Lego robots, or even go on summer camps abroad; But what about children from poor families? What they can access might only be an old phone and free video apps.

It’s not that they don’t love learning; it’s that they don’t have anything else to do. It’s not that they lack self-discipline; it’s that their world is too small, too noisy, and too lonely.

Playing on the phone is not decadence; it is an alternative solution to resource scarcity.

🎓【III】What truly determines grades is not self-discipline, but the parents’ “Invisible Power”

We always assume that a child’s good grades rely on their self-control. But actually:

  • Where does self-control come from? It comes from the subtle influence absorbed from the family environment.
  • Self-discipline is not a talent; it is a habit, and the shaping of habits relies on long-term companionship and guidance.

And who is best equipped to provide that guidance? Naturally, the parents. But this brings us back to the old question:

  • Parents in affluent families: They have time, education, and patience; they can accompany their children to study, discuss, and plan for the future;
  • Parents in ordinary or low-income families: They are exhausted from work, emotionally unstable, and sometimes lack the ability to help with homework, let alone plan for growth.

It’s not that they don’t want to teach; it’s that they lack the time, the energy, and the conditions.

📊【IV】It’s not the phone that ruins the child; it’s structural poverty that traps the family

What we need to see is a deeper reality:

The phone cannot ruin a child, but “time poverty + mental exhaustion + resource shortage” can.

We are not fighting the phone; we are fighting social inequality, family anxiety, and parental helplessness.

Not everyone can send their child to an elite school, but every family can begin by achieving self-awareness, rebuilding their capacity for companionship, critical thinking, and growth.

🚀【V】The one who truly needs to be in the rat race is ourselves, not the child

Instead of constantly “pushing” the child (chicken-raising), why don’t we ask ourselves:

  • Have we made efforts to improve the family’s economic foundation?
  • Have we learned how to be an emotionally stable, loving, and patient parent?
  • Have we put down our phones and anxiety to truly see the child’s emotions and growth?
  • Have we lived and grown with effort, setting a living example for our child?

We are too quick to get angry at our children, yet too slow to ask ourselves questions. We are too quick to worry about the future, yet unwilling to change the present.

True “chicken-raising” is not about squeezing the child; it is about awakening the parent.

🧭【Conclusion: The bigger your world, the further your child’s future will reach】

The child is not a tool for your return on investment; they are the continuation of your life attitude.

The best thing we can give our children is not anxiety, not control, and not banning the phone, but:

  • A loving home;
  • A growth process that is being listened to;
  • A role model of parents who are continuously striving and growing.

Stop pushing the child. Start pushing yourself. Change truly begins there.
